native_result.query: The effect of which variable on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024 to 0.0923 (while becoming insignifcant) when both SES and academic characteristics are included in analysis?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of SES on BA degree completion decreases from 0.3636  (significant) to  -0.2293 (insignificant) and effect of race on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024  (significant) to 0.0923 (insignificant) when academic characteristics are considered.
native_result.HypoB: The variable is the respondent's race (SAMPLE_RACE) — the White-vs-non-White contrast. The log-odds effect of being White on BA degree completion is large and significant on its own (+0.9735, p<0.0001) but collapses ~13x to +0.0741 (p=0.68, not significant, ~ the target 0.0923) once SES and academic characteristics (ASVAB composite score and class percentile) are controlled — i.e., the racial gap in BA completion is largely explained by socioeconomic status and academic preparation.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection: N=8773, 9 columns, zero missingness; BA rate 2.7%; all point-biserial correlations with BA <=0.18 so effects read as logistic coefficients. 2) Two-model design: A = bivariate logit of BA on each focal; B = BA ~ focal + SES + ASVAB + PERCENTILE (canonical), with sensitivity variants (academics={PCT},{ASVAB},{both}; +social background; logit/probit/OLS). 3) Enumerated focals: RACE(White/Black/Hispanic/Minority), SEX, FAMILY SIZE, SES, ASVAB, PERCENTILE. 4) Scored each on proximity to bivariate 0.5024, full-model ~0.00-0.15 with p>0.05, positive sign, consistency with 'SES-as-control' wording. 5) Result: RACE (White vs non-White) is the only social-background focal (SES as control) that collapses to ~0.07-0.00 (ns) — only when BOTH academic characteristics enter; FAMILY SIZE disqualified (no decline), SES runner-up (numeric fit but excluded by wording and sign-flip under canonical model). 6) Score table and script saved as artifacts.
